narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 69.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest negative influence. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school—far below the average of roughly sixth decile among accepted students. These unusually low academic standings strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 37 was the next most important factor; it was only slightly below the average of accepted students and therefore worked modestly in the opposite direction, pulling the prediction slightly toward passing.

Taken together, the very weak class rankings outweighed the near-average LSAT and led the model to conclude you were unlikely to pass the bar. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.5 (versus 3.23 for accepted students), middle family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the outcome.

You should focus on improving your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to raise both your class rank and test score. Strengthening these two areas will give you the best chance of a favorable prediction on a future application. (198 words)
